source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: A test cross of a plant showing a dominant monohybrid phenotype is made with a
questions.explanation: Crossing with the double (or single) recessive tester reveals whether the dominant parent is hetero- or homozygous.

questions.stem: Independent assortment is expected when two genes lie on
options: the same chromatid with zero map distance
the Y chromosome of every female
questions.explanation: Genes on different chromosome pairs segregate independently at anaphase I.

questions.stem: Incomplete dominance of flower colour in snapdragon gives an F2 phenotypic ratio of
questions.explanation: Heterozygotes are intermediate, so phenotypes track the 1:2:1 genotypic split.

questions.stem: The ABO blood-group locus is a classic example of
questions.explanation: More than two alleles (IA, IB, i) exist in the population, though a person carries only two.

questions.stem: In humans the heterogametic sex is the
questions.explanation: Human males produce two kinds of gametes (X or Y) and are therefore heterogametic.

questions.stem: A colour-blind father married to a homozygous normal mother is expected to have
questions.explanation: The father passes Xc to every daughter (carriers) and Y to every son, who receive a normal X from the mother.

questions.stem: Genes that do not assort independently because they occupy one chromosome are said to be
questions.explanation: Linkage keeps genes on the same chromosome together unless crossing over separates them.

questions.stem: Klinefelter syndrome in humans is associated with the karyotype
questions.explanation: An extra X in a phenotypic male (XXY) produces Klinefelter syndrome; 45, X is Turner.

questions.stem: Insertion or deletion of a single nucleotide that shifts the codon reading frame is a
questions.explanation: Indels not in multiples of three alter every codon downstream and usually destroy the protein.

questions.stem: Alternative forms of a gene that occupy the same locus on homologues are called
questions.explanation: Alleles are variants of one gene; a diploid individual carries two alleles of each autosomal gene.

questions.stem: The F2 genotypic ratio of a monohybrid Mendelian self-cross is
questions.explanation: AA : Aa : aa = 1 : 2 : 1; the 3 : 1 ratio is phenotypic when dominance is complete.

questions.stem: Haemophilia is more frequent in males because the defective allele is
options: recessive and located on the X chromosome
always Y-linked and lethal in embryos
mitochondrial and transmitted by fathers only
questions.explanation: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes, so a single recessive allele is expressed.

questions.stem: A woman with Turner syndrome has
questions.explanation: Turner females lack one sex chromosome (45, X) and are sterile with characteristic somatic features.

questions.stem: A tall pea plant of unknown genotype crossed with dwarf (tt) yields half dwarf progeny. The tall parent is
questions.explanation: A 1 : 1 tall : dwarf split is the test-cross signature of a heterozygote.

questions.stem: If genes assort independently, a dihybrid test cross AaBb × aabb is expected to give phenotypic proportions
questions.explanation: The tester contributes only ab gametes, so four equally frequent progeny classes appear.

questions.stem: A person of genotype IAIB expresses both A and B antigens. This pattern is
questions.explanation: IA and IB are co-dominant: both glycolipid antigens appear on the red-cell surface.

questions.stem: A person of blood group O must have the genotype
questions.explanation: Group O lacks A and B antigens and is homozygous for the recessive allele i.

questions.stem: Birds typically show which sex-chromosome pattern?
options: XO male as in some insects only
questions.explanation: In birds the female is heterogametic (ZW) and the male is ZZ.

questions.stem: A pedigree of an X-linked recessive trait typically shows
options: more affected males and no father-to-son transmission
equal affected sexes in every generation
questions.explanation: Sons get their X from the mother; an affected father passes his X only to daughters.

questions.stem: Crossing over that recombines linked genes occurs during
questions.explanation: Reciprocal chiasmata form between homologous chromatids at pachytene.

questions.stem: Which condition is a sex-chromosomal aneuploidy rather than an autosomal trisomy?
questions.explanation: Turner is 45, X; Down, Patau and Edwards are trisomies 21, 13 and 18.

questions.stem: A chromosomal inversion
options: reverses a segment within a chromosome
adds an entire extra haploid set
is the same as a frameshift in one codon
questions.explanation: An inverted block remains on the same chromosome; gene order, not copy number, is changed.

questions.stem: The observable traits of an organism in a given environment constitute its
questions.explanation: Phenotype is the expressed character; genotype is the allelic constitution.

questions.stem: Mendel's law of dominance is illustrated when a tall × dwarf true-breeding cross yields
options: an F1 that is uniformly tall
an F1 that is uniformly dwarf
alleles that never separate in meiosis
questions.explanation: The dominant allele masks the recessive one in the heterozygote, so F1 shows the tall phenotype.

questions.stem: Which statement about classical haemophilia is incorrect?
options: It is autosomally dominant and equally common in both sexes
It is an X-linked recessive clotting defect
Affected males transmit the allele to all daughters
Heterozygous females are usually phenotypically normal carriers
questions.explanation: Haemophilia A/B is X-linked recessive, not autosomal dominant, which is why males are affected far more often.

questions.stem: Cri-du-chat syndrome is associated with
options: deletion of a portion of the short arm of chromosome 5
questions.explanation: A 5p deletion produces the cat-like cry and developmental features of cri-du-chat.
